notes.short: A saying: “The harvest has passed”
notes.about: The people cry out: “The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.” The words are read as a common saying of hope that failed: season after season went by, and the rescue they looked for never came.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: The harvest has passed, the summer has ended
figure.means: one hope of rescue after another has gone by with the seasons, and no rescue has come

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke says the words seem to have been a proverb: deliverance was looked for one year, then the next, and none came. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls them proverbial: one season of hope after another passed with no deliverance. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) says the whole saying had probably become proverbial for the deepest misery.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the seasons stand for: the years of a siege, a year of famine, or one hope after another. Two of them hold the words only likely to be a proverb.

cites.quote: This seems to have been a proverb: "We expected deliverance the first year - none came. We hoped for it the second year - we are disappointed; we are not saved - no deliverance is come."
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Proverbial. Meaning: One season of hope after another has passed, but the looked-for deliverance never came, and now all hope is gone.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: They are as men in a year of famine — “The harvest is past,” and there has been no crop for men to reap. ... All has failed alike. The whole formula had probably become proverbial for extremest misery.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A saying: “Destroy the tree with its fruit”
notes.about: Jeremiah learns of a plot against his life and quotes the plotters' words: “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit.” The next words say plainly what the saying means: “let us cut him off from the land of the living.” Many read the tree as the prophet and the fruit as his message.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: Let us destroy the tree with its fruit
figure.means: kill Jeremiah outright, and with him put an end to the message he brought

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry calls it a proverbial expression: destroy the prophet and his prophecy, or perhaps the man and his family. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it figurative or proverbial, put plainly in the next clause. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): proverbial, the man the tree, his teaching the fruit. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott): proverbial for ending the man and his work.
notes.limit: One of the writers allows that the fruit may be the prophet's family, though he prefers his message.

cites.quote: They said concerning Jeremiah, Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof—a proverbial expression, meaning, "Let us utterly destroy him root and branch. Let us destroy both the father and the family" (as, when Naboth was put to death for treason, his sons were put to death with him), or rather "both the prophet and the prophecy; let us kill the one and defeat the other.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: In like manner Jeremiah had no suspicion that his countrymen were harbouring evil designs against him. ... The saying is a figurative or proverbial one: we will destroy the tree ... The proverbial saying is given in plain words in the next clause. We will cut him (i.e., the prophet) off, etc.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Proverbial, to express the destruction of cause and effect together. The man is the tree; his teaching, the fruit. Let us destroy the prophet and his prophecies; namely, those threatening destruction to the nation, which offended them.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Literally, the tree with its bread, here taken for its “fruit.” ... The phrase would seem to be proverbial for total destruction, not of the man only, but of his work.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Racing men on foot, then horses
notes.about: The LORD answers Jeremiah's complaint with two sayings. If men on foot have worn him out, how can he compete with horses? If he stumbles in a peaceful land, how will he do in the thickets of the Jordan? The trials he has met are small beside those still to come.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: If you have raced with men on foot and they have worn you out, how can you compete with horses?
figure.means: if lesser trials have worn him out, how will he bear the far greater ones still to come

notes.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) says the LORD rebukes Jeremiah's impatience by two proverbial sayings: greater trials of faith are in store. Adam Clarke calls the words proverbial: if small evils make him complain, what of great ones? A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a proverbial phrase, the men of Anathoth the men on foot and those of Jerusalem the horsemen.
notes.limit: The writers differ on who the men on foot and the horses stand for, such as the men of Anathoth and of Jerusalem, or lesser and greater enemies, and on whether the Jordan's thickets point to its floods or to its lions.

cites.quote: Yahweh rebukes Jeremiah's impatience, showing him by two proverbial sayings, that there were still greater trials of faith in store for him. Prosperous wickedness is after all a mere ordinary trial, a mere "running with the footmen;" he will have to exert far greater powers of endurance.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: If the smallest evils to which thou art exposed cause thee to make so many bitter complaints, how wilt thou feel when, in the course of thy prophetic ministry, thou shalt be exposed to much greater, from enemies much more powerful? ... But still the words are proverbial, and the above is their meaning.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: horses--that is, horsemen: the argument a fortiori. A proverbial phrase. The injuries done thee by the men of Anathoth ("the footmen") are small compared with those which the men of Jerusalem ("the horsemen") are about to inflict on thee.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A ruined loincloth acts out Judah's fate
notes.about: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a linen loincloth and wear it, then hide it in a crevice of the rocks at Perath. Many days later he digs it up, ruined. Verses 9 to 11 explain the act: the LORD made His people cling to Him like a loincloth, and now He will ruin their pride.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: hide it there in a crevice of the rocks
figure.means: Judah sent away into exile, where its pride would be ruined as the hidden loincloth was

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a symbolical action really carried out, the loincloth an emblem of Israel, its decay by the Euphrates the ruin of the people. Matthew Henry calls it a sign, sees no difficulty in two journeys, and ties the Euphrates to Babylon, the place of bondage. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott) says placing the girdle by the Euphrates stood for the seventy years of exile.
notes.limit: Some readers hold that the journeys to Perath took place in a vision rather than in fact; the writers cited take the act as really done, and take Perath as the Euphrates.

cites.quote: With regard to the symbolical action imposed on the prophet and performed by him ... pointing as it does to a literal and real carrying out of God's command ... the girdle is the emblem of Israel ... the mouldering of the girdle in the earth by the Euphrates signifies not the moral but the physical decay of the covenant people
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A sign, the marring of a girdle, which the prophet had worn for some time, by hiding it in a hole of a rock near the river Euphrates. It was usual with the prophets to teach by signs ... I see no inconvenience in supposing the prophet to have made two journeys thither ... Euphrates being the river of Babylon, which was to be the place of their bondage, was a material circumstance in this sign.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Here again the interval is undefined, but it must have been long enough (we may conjecture, perhaps, seventy days) to be an adequate symbol of the seventy years’ exile which the act of placing the girdle by Euphrates represented.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A likeness: every wineskin filled with wine
notes.about: The LORD gives Jeremiah a saying so plain that the people scoff at it: “Every wineskin shall be filled with wine.” Then He applies it to them. He will fill all who live in the land with drunkenness, from the kings down, and smash them against one another. The drunkenness stands for His wrath.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Every wineskin shall be filled with wine
figure.means: the people of the land, whom God will fill with the drunkenness of His wrath as jars are filled with wine, and then break

original.note: In Hebrew the word for wineskin can also mean an earthen wine jar, which fits the smashing of verse 14.

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it a similitude: the people knew bottles held wine, but not that they were like bottles. Henry says the doom is given in a figure: sinners filled with God's wrath as a bottle is with wine. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) makes the jar an emblem of man, filled by God with the wine of His wrath. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a new image: God's wrath intoxicates like wine.
notes.limit: The saying itself has no word for like: the likeness comes out when the LORD applies it in verses 13 and 14. Writers differ on whether the vessel is a skin or an earthen jar.

cites.quote: The Prophet denounces here by another similitude the vengeance of God, for he says that all would be filled with drunkenness ... They indeed, all knew that bottles were made for wine; but they did not understand that they were the bottles, or were like bottles.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This doom is pronounced against them in a figure, to make it the more taken notice of and the more affecting ... every bottle shall be filled with wine; that is, those that by their sins have made themselves vessels of wrath fitted to destruction shall be filled with the wrath of God as a bottle is with wine
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: an earthenware vessel, especially the wine jar (cf. Isa 30:24 ; Lam 4:2 ), is here the emblem of man ... As one fills all wine jars, so must all inhabitants of the land be filled by God with wine of intoxication. Drunkenness is the effect of the intoxicating wine of God's wrath ... I dash them one against the other, as jars are shivered when knocked together.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: A new image. ... The figurative sense which is what Jeremiah chiefly meant, they affected not to understand. As wine intoxicates, so God's wrath and judgments shall reduce them to that state of helpless distraction that they shall rush on to their own ruin
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Land, land, land”: one call said three times
notes.about: The prophet calls on the land three times in a row. The repetition gives the call its weight and draws close attention to the solemn and certain word that follows about Coniah and his line (verse 30). It can also be read as hammer blows on a people hardened against God's warnings.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.words: land, land, land
figure.means: a call made three times, to give it weight and make the land heed the solemn word that follows

original.note: In Hebrew the word said three times is erets, which can mean land or earth.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis, a word repeated to mark it and draw attention. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the triple summons gives it special emphasis and marks what follows as weighty. Benson: the word is repeated for emphasis and deeper attention. Plumptre (Ellicott): the solemn repetition shows the decree is certain. Calvin likens it to hammer strokes on hardened hearts.

cites.quote: It is a common and powerful way of emphasizing a particular word, by thus marking it and calling attention to it.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The land is to take the king's fate sore to heart. The triple repetition of the summons: Land, gives it a special emphasis, and marks the following sentence as of high importance
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the repetition was not superfluous in exclaiming “earth” three times, for as the hardness of iron is overcome by the repeated strokes of the hammer, so the Prophet repeated the word “earth,” that he might subdue that perverseness in which the Jews had so hardened themselves that no threats of God moved them.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The word earth, or land rather, as ארצ may be properly rendered, is repeated three times by way of emphasis, to engage the deeper attention.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: The solemnity of the mystic threefold repetition expresses the certainty of the Divine decree
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: A question that answers itself: they cannot change
notes.about: The LORD asks a question with only one answer. An Ethiopian cannot change his skin, nor a leopard its spots, and Judah, long trained in evil, can no more turn and do good by itself. Doing evil had become as fixed in them as the color of a skin.

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.words: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
figure.means: those long used to doing evil can no more turn and do good than a skin or spots can change

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Erotesis, questions about what cannot be. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the question denies the very thing it raises, so the one is as impossible as the other. Henry, Calvin and Plumptre (Ellicott) say Judah's evil had grown too fixed for it to reform. Clarke agrees the skin cannot change but reads the moral point as extreme difficulty.
notes.limit: Most take the change as impossible for Judah; one reads it as extremely hard and seldom seen. Some add that God's grace can do what man cannot, and verse 27 still pleads with Jerusalem to be made clean. The verse speaks of people trained in evil by long practice.

cites.at: Erotesis, in Absurdities and Impossibilities, p. 956
cites.quote: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23 ). See Parœmia .
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The consequential clause introduced by גּם אתּם connects with the possibility suggested in, but denied by, the preceding question: if that could happen, then might even ye do good. The one thing is as impossible as the other.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, that is by nature black, or the leopard his spots, that are even woven into the skin? Dirt contracted may be washed off, but we cannot alter the natural colour of a hair ... much less of the skin; and so impossible is it, morally impossible, to reclaim and reform these people.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: God declares in this verse, that the people were so hardened in their wickedness, that there was no hope of their repentance. ... he says that they could not repent, that wickedness had become inherent, or firmly fixed in their hearts, like the blackness which is inherent in the skin of the Ethiopians
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The meaning of the question is obvious. The evil of Judah was too deep-ingrained to be capable of spontaneous reformation.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: These things are natural to them, and they cannot be altered; so sin, and especially your attachment to idolatry, is become a second nature ... But the expression does not imply that the thing is as impossible in a moral as it is in a natural sense: it only shows that it is extremely difficult, and not to be often expected
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A saying: can the leopard change his spots?
notes.about: The verse asks two questions whose plain answer is no: can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? It then applies them: those accustomed to doing evil are not able to do good. The questions are read as a saying first found here that has since passed into common use.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
figure.means: as the Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the leopard his spots, so those accustomed to doing evil are not able to do good

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the two questions under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use as proverbs. The verse itself applies them to those accustomed to doing evil.
notes.limit: The verse itself does not call the questions a proverb; they count as one because the saying has since passed into common use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: Jeremiah's life as a sign: no wife, no mourning
notes.about: The LORD forbids Jeremiah to marry and have children, to go into a house where there is a funeral meal, or to sit down at a feast. His own life carries the message: children born in the land will die unmourned, mourning itself will cease, and the voices of bride and bridegroom will be silenced.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: You must not marry or have sons or daughters in this place
figure.means: the coming disaster will be so great that marriage and children, and even mourning and feasting, will give way to it

notes.evidence: Henry says the prophet is here for a sign to the people, forbearing marriage, mourning and mirth as one who expects the ruin. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) calls the ban on marriage a sign that the calamity would override all ordinary duties. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says he adapts his actions to convey his message. Calvin finds the ban full of meaning, and his single life likely a living sign.
notes.limit: One writer says the command came in a vision and leaves open whether Jeremiah stayed unmarried, though he thinks it probable that he did, so that his single life was itself a sign.

cites.quote: The prophet is here for a sign to the people. They would not regard what he said; let it be tried whether they will regard what he does. ... Others go on in their usual course, but he, in the prospect of these sad times, is forbidden and therefore forbears marriage, mourning for the dead, and mirth.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: As marriage was obligatory upon the Jews, the prohibition of it to Jeremiah was a sign that the impending calamity was so great as to override all ordinary duties.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He is both to abstain from the customary usages of mourning for the dead, and to keep away from mirthful feasts, in order to give the people to understand that, by reason of the multitude of the dead, customary mourning will have to be given up, and that all opportunity for merry-making will disappear ... Adapting thus his actions to help to convey his message
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: But the prohibition to marry was full of meaning; it was to shew that the people were wholly given up to destruction. ... he received this command in a vision; and though he might not have been unmarried, he might still have proclaimed this prophecy ... his celibacy might have been intended to be, as it were, a living representation, in order to produce an effect on the Jews.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Cursed and like a shrub; blessed and like a tree
notes.about: A curse on the man who trusts in mankind is followed by a picture of him, a shrub in the desert. A blessing on the man who trusts in the LORD is followed by its picture, a tree planted by the waters.

lines.words: Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind,
He will be like a shrub in the desert;
But blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD,
He is like a tree planted by the waters

notes.evidence: Boys sets the four verses out in four members that take turns: a curse and a blessing in the first and third, and a confirmation or reason for each in the second and fourth.

cites.quote: Here we have a curse and a blessing in A. and A.; and a confirmation, or reason for each, in B. and B. … The leading terms very distinctly mark out for us the arrangement of the passage.
cites.read: the 1825 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/akeytobookpsalm00boysgoog

notes.short: A saying: the partridge hatching eggs not its own
notes.about: The verse sets the man who makes a fortune unjustly beside a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay. It is read as a common saying of the day: as the young hatched from another bird's eggs leave her, his riches desert him in the middle of his days, and in the end he is the fool.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: Like a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay is the man who makes a fortune unjustly
figure.means: riches gained unjustly leave the man who gained them, as the young hatched from eggs not her own leave the bird

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a common saying joined to verse 10: the proverb likens the man who gains riches by wrong to a partridge hatching eggs it did not lay, whose young forsake her. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) says a popular belief about the bird made it a parable of the covetous man, whose riches fly away.
notes.limit: The verse does not call itself a saying: it is read as one in common use, built on a belief of the day about the bird and applied to the man who gains riches unjustly.

cites.quote: With this is joined the common saying as to the partridge, Jer 17:11 . ... The proverb ran: He that gains riches, and that by wrong, i.e., in an unjust, dishonourable manner, is like a partridge which hatches eggs it has not laid. ... The point of the comparison, that the young hatched out of another bird's eggs forsake the mother, is brought out in the application of the proverb.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The words point to a popular belief among the Jews that the partridge steals the eggs of other birds and adds them to her own, with the result that when the eggs are hatched the broods desert her ... It thus became a parable of the covetous man, whose avarice leads him to pile up riches which are not rightly his, and which after a while “make to themselves wings” and are seen no more.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: Jeremiah shatters a clay jar before the elders
notes.about: The LORD sends Jeremiah to buy a clay jar, take elders and priests to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, and proclaim disaster for their idolatry. Then he is to shatter the jar before them. The act shows what the LORD will do: He will shatter the nation and the city like a jar that can never be repaired.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: you are to shatter the jar in the presence of the men who accompany you
figure.means: the LORD will break the nation and the city past mending, as a fired clay jar once shattered can never be made whole

notes.evidence: Henry says a visible sign enforces the message, its hearers made its spectators. Calvin: a sign that sealed the prophecy by a visible act. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a symbolical action, explained in verse 11. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) sets this symbol against the clay of 18:4: clay can be reshaped, a broken jar cannot. Clarke: a symbolical representation of the city's ruin.

cites.quote: By a visible sign. The prophet was to take along with him an earthen bottle ... and, when he had delivered his message, he was to break the bottle to pieces ... and the same that were auditors of the sermon must be spectators of the sign.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: There was not only importance in the sign, that they might thence learn the doom of the city and of the whole land, but it was also a solemn sealing of the prophecy; and on this account he was commanded to break the vessel, even that he might show, by a visible act, the near approach of God’s vengeance, of which the Jews had no apprehension.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: break . . . bottle--a symbolical action, explained in Jer 19:11 .
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In this lies the distinction between this symbol and that of Jer 18:4 . The plastic clay can be shaped and re-shaped until the potter forms with it the vessel he had predetermined: the broken bottle is of no further use, but its fragments are cast away forever upon the heaps of rubbish deposited in Tophet.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Even so will I break this people and this city - The breaking of the bottle was the symbolical representation of the destruction of the city and of the state.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A saying: what is straw compared to grain?
notes.about: The LORD has spoken of prophets who prophesy lies in His name, saying, “I had a dream!” (verse 25). Let the dreamer retell his dream, He says, and the one with His word speak it truthfully. Then He asks a question that later became a common saying: “For what is straw compared to grain?”

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: what is straw compared to grain
figure.means: a saying that straw is nothing beside grain; the verse sets the prophet's dream beside the LORD's word

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the question under Parœmia, among proverbs that first appear in Scripture and have since come into common use as sayings. The verses around it (23:25-27 and 32) tell of prophets who prophesy lies and false dreams in the LORD's name, and the verse sets their dreams beside His word.
notes.limit: The verse does not call the question a saying; it is counted one because it later came into common use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “What is the chaff (Heb., straw) to the wheat?”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: A byword: “What is the burden of the LORD?”
notes.about: The prophets called a message from God a burden. The people, and even prophets and priests, made the word a byword, asking, “What is the burden of the LORD?” in scorn of His threats. The LORD forbids it: they are to ask what He has answered or spoken, for each man's word becomes the burden.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: What is the burden of the LORD?
figure.means: a mocking catchword that called the LORD's word a burden, as if He sent nothing but threats

original.note: In Hebrew the word for burden is also the word for a solemn message from God, a prophecy.

notes.evidence: Calvin says that in their hatred they called God's word a burden and used it as a proverbial saying, in the ways and streets. Henry says the scoffers took the prophets' word and made a jest and a byword of it, so that it would no longer make people serious.
notes.limit: The verses do not call the question a byword: it is read as one because scoffers had made the prophets' solemn word a common jest. The prophets themselves had used the word seriously.

cites.quote: Now, a burden means a prophecy, which terrifies the despisers of God by threatening them with vengeance. As, then, their minds were exasperated, they called through hatred the word of God a burden, and used it as a proverbial saying, “It is a burden, a burden.” ... It was surely a most shameful thing, that the word of God should be thus called in disdain and contempt, in the ways and streets
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: This was the word that gave great offence to God, that, whenever they spoke of the word of the Lord, they called it, in scorn and derision, the burden of the Lord. ... Now the profane scoffers took this word, and made a jest and a byword of it; they made people merry with it, that so, when the prophets used it, they might not make people serious with it.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: The cup of the LORD's wrath handed to the nations
notes.about: The LORD tells Jeremiah to take the cup of the wine of His wrath and make the nations drink from it, Jerusalem and Judah first. They will stagger because of the sword He will send among them (verse 16). Many read the act as done in vision, or by Jeremiah declaring the judgment, not with a real cup.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: I took the cup from the LORD’s hand and made all the nations drink from it
figure.means: the judgment God would bring on Judah first and then on the nations, His punishment for their sins

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the whole action is emblematical of a real work of God on kings and peoples, carried out when Jeremiah announced it. Clarke says the cup is symbolical and means Jeremiah declared that the nations would fall under the Chaldeans as God's punishment. Plumptre (Ellicott) and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) say the act took place in vision.
notes.limit: The writers hold that no real cup was handed round. Some read the act as seen in vision; others say Jeremiah carried it out by proclaiming the judgment in Jerusalem.

cites.quote: As the wrath of God is no essence that may be drunk by the bodily act, so manifestly the cup is no material cup, and the drinking of it no act of the outer, physical reality. The whole action is accordingly only emblematical of a real work of God wrought on kings and peoples, and is performed by Jeremiah when he announces what he is commanded.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This cup of God's wrath is merely symbolical, and simply means that the prophet should declare to all these people that they shall fall under the Chaldean yoke, and that this is a punishment inflicted on them by God for their iniquities.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The words describe the act of the prophet as in the ecstasy of vision. One by one the nations are made to drink of that cup of the wrath of Jehovah of which His own country was to have the first and fullest draught.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: wine cup--Compare Jer 13:12-13 , as to this image, to express stupefying judgments ... The wine cup was not literally given by Jeremiah to the representatives of the different nations; but only in symbolical vision.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Jeremiah wears a yoke: serve Babylon and live
notes.about: The LORD tells Jeremiah to make a yoke and wear it, and to send word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon. The yoke shows that the nations must serve Nebuchadnezzar. To Zedekiah he says, “Put your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon; serve him and his people, and live!”

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: Make for yourself a yoke out of leather straps and put it on your neck
figure.means: the yoke of Babylon that Judah and the nations around it must bear, serving Nebuchadnezzar

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls the yoke a plain emblem of the Babylonian yoke the nations are to bear, and says Jeremiah really wore it (28:10). Clarke calls it a symbolical action, showing that the kings named would come under the Chaldeans. Henry calls it a sign and a prophetic representation of those lands brought under the king of Babylon.
notes.limit: Some of the writers add that Jeremiah also made yokes for the five kings' envoys; the BSB says only that he sent them word.

cites.quote: The yoke Jeremiah is to make and lay on his neck is a plain emblem of the Babylonian yoke the nations are to bear. ... That Jeremiah really put such a yoke on his neck and wore it, we see from Jer 28:10 , Jer 28:12 , where a false prophet breaks it for him.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Make thee bonds and yokes - Probably yokes with straps, by which they were attached to the neck. This was a symbolical action, to show that the several kings mentioned below should be brought under the dominion of the Chaldeans.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Jeremiah is to prepare a sign of the general reduction of all these countries into subjection to the king of Babylon ... Into these the prophet must put his own neck to make them taken notice of as a prophetic representation; for every one would enquire, What is the meaning of Jeremiah's yokes?
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Hananiah breaks the yoke; God answers with iron
notes.about: The prophet Hananiah takes the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and breaks it, saying that in this way the LORD will break Nebuchadnezzar's yoke within two years. The LORD answers that Hananiah has broken a yoke of wood but fashioned a yoke of iron: the nations will serve Babylon.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: took the yoke off the neck of Jeremiah the prophet and broke it
figure.means: a counter-sign meant to promise the people that Babylon's yoke would soon be broken; the LORD turns it into a yoke of iron

notes.evidence: Clarke says Hananiah tried by this symbolical act to persuade the people; Henry, that he broke it to give a sign, as Jeremiah had given of his; R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes), that the crowd would see a symbol of deliverance in it. Calvin says by that representation he made them expect deliverance in two years. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the LORD's answer shows Babylon's yoke is iron.
notes.limit: Hananiah's sign was false: the LORD had not sent him (verse 15), and the broken yoke of wood only led to a yoke of iron.

cites.quote: Then Hananiah - took the yoke - and brake it - He endeavored by this symbolical act to persuade them of the truth of his prediction.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: he took the yoke from off his neck which he carried as a memorial of what he had prophesied concerning the enslaving of the nations to Nebuchadnezzar, and he broke it, that he might give a sign of the accomplishment of this prophecy, as Jeremiah had given of his, and might seem to have conquered him
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The multitude would see in Hananiah's act a symbol of deliverance.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: laying sacrilegious hands on that visible symbol, by which it had pleased God to testify that the Prophet’s message was true. ... he not only took away that sign, but by breaking the bands he attracted the attention of men, and by such a representation made them to believe that there would be in two years a deliverance.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: he gives the deeper meaning of that occurrence. By breaking Jeremiah's wooden yoke, Hananiah has only signified that the yoke Nebuchadnezzar lays on the nations will not be so easily broken as a wooden one, but is of iron, i.e., not to be broken.

notes.short: A curse the exiles would use: like Zedekiah and Ahab
notes.about: Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah prophesied lies to the exiles (verse 21). The king of Babylon would put them to death in the fire, and the exiles would curse with their fate: “May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab.” Their death can be read as passing into a common saying.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.words: May the LORD make you like Zedekiah and Ahab
figure.means: a set curse wishing on someone the death by fire of the two lying prophets

original.note: In Hebrew the word for curse, qelalah, sounds like qalah, roasted, which may be why the saying took hold.

notes.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) says the death of these men passed into a proverb, probably because of a play on words: they are made a curse (qelalah) because Nebuchadnezzar roasted (qalah) them, and one of them was the son of Kolaiah.
notes.limit: The verse itself calls the words a curse; they count as a saying because all the exiles in Babylon would use them.

cites.quote: A curse - There is a play here of words. which probably was the cause why the death of these men passed into a proverb. One of them was named ben-Kolaiah; and they are to be made a curse (קללה qelâlâh), because Nebuchadnezzar had roasted (קלה qâlâh) them.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A saying that blamed the fathers for the children
notes.about: People said that the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth were set on edge, meaning they suffered for their fathers' sins, not their own. It can be read as a charge that God was unjust. The LORD says it will be said no more: instead, “each will die for his own iniquity” (verse 30).

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge
figure.means: the children are punished for their fathers' sins, not for their own

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists it under Parœmia, a proverb already in use, and points to Ezekiel 18:2-3. Calvin says the people used it to strive with God, as if He punished them while innocent; Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) reads it as a complaint that God is unjust. Plumptre (Ellicott) says it was in common use and eased their consciences; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the exiles' children used it.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: “In those days they shall say no more, ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’ ” This is what they did once say. See Eze 18:2-3.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Ezekiel shews that it was a complaint commonly prevailing among the people, that they suffered for the sins of their fathers ... Such, then, was the arrogance of the Jews, as to strive with God, as though he punished them, while they were innocent; and they expressed this by using a proverb
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: The proverb means, "Children atone for the misdeeds of their fathers," or "The sins of the fathers are visited on their innocent children." ... The proverb mentioned in Jer 31:29 involves the complaint against God, that in punishing sin He deals unjustly.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The proverb was one which, as we find from Eze 18:2-3 , had at this time come into common use. Men found in it an explanation of their sufferings which relieved their consciences. They were suffering, they said, for the sins of their fathers, not for their own.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: the proverb among the exiles' children born in Babylon, to express that they suffered the evil consequences of their fathers' sins rather than of their own
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Jeremiah buys a field while Jerusalem is besieged
notes.about: While Babylon's army besieges Jerusalem and Jeremiah is held in the courtyard of the guard, the LORD has him buy his cousin Hanamel's field at Anathoth, with deeds signed before witnesses and kept in a clay jar. The act shows that “Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.”

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: So I bought the field in Anathoth from my cousin Hanamel
figure.means: the people would return from exile and own land in Judah again, so a purchase made in faith of that was safe

notes.evidence: Clarke says the whole was designed as a symbolical act, showing there would be a return from Babylon and each family would re-enter its lands. Calvin speaks of the external symbol showing that the Jews would return to their land. Henry says the bargain was made to signify that the land would be possessed again; Keil (Keil and Delitzsch), that the purchase meant Judah would return to its land.

cites.quote: This was the word of the Lord - It was by his appointment that I was to make this purchase. The whole was designed as a symbolical act, to show the people that there would be a return from Babylon, that each family should re-enter on its former possessions, and that a man might safely purchase on the certainty of this event.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The whole of this passage ought to be read together, for the Prophet at large explains how and by what symbol this prophecy had been confirmed. ... Let us now come to the external symbol. The Prophet was commanded to buy a field of his uncle’s son. ... But in this way God intended to shew, that after the Jews had for a time been deprived of the possession of the land, they would again return to it
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: What was the design of having this bargain made. It was to signify that though Jerusalem was now besieged, and the whole country was likely to be laid waste, yet the time should come when houses, and fields, and vineyards should be again possessed in this land
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: There is also implied the intimation, that the present desolation of the land and the transportation of its inhabitants will only last during their time; and then the population of Judah will return, and enter again on the possession of their land. The purchase of the field on the part of Jeremiah had this meaning; and for the sake of this meaning it was announced to him by God
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: Wine set before the Rechabites, who will not drink
notes.about: God sends Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into the temple and set wine before them. They refuse, since their forefather Jonadab forbade it. God then sets their faithfulness to a man against Judah: “But I have spoken to you again and again, and you have not obeyed Me!”

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: I set pitchers full of wine and some cups before the men of the house of the Rechabites
figure.means: a test whose answer shamed Judah: the Rechabites kept a dead man's command, while God's own people would not obey God

notes.evidence: Matthew Henry says the trial of the Rechabites' constancy was meant as a sign, which God then applies to the Jews, so that they may see it and be ashamed. Calvin says a visible sign was needed to shame a careless people, who would not obey God while the Rechabites obeyed their father, a mortal man long dead.
notes.limit: Verses 18 and 19 add God's promise to the Rechabites themselves. The note keeps to the sign set before Judah.

cites.quote: The trial of the Rechabites' constancy was intended but for a sign; now here we have the application of it. I. The Rechabites' observance of their father's charge to them is made use of as an aggravation of the disobedience of the Jews to God. Let them see it and be ashamed.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: As, then, their security kept them from being attentive to the words of the Prophet, it was necessary to set before them a visible sign, in order to make them ashamed. It was, then, God’s purpose to shew how inexcusable was their perverseness. This was the design of this prophecy.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Stones hidden at Pharaoh's door for Babylon's throne
notes.about: At Tahpanhes in Egypt, where the Jews had fled, God tells Jeremiah to bury large stones at the entrance to Pharaoh's palace while the Jews watch. Then God explains the act: “I will set his throne over these stones that I have embedded.” The king of Babylon would come and strike down Egypt.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: bury them in the clay of the brick pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh’s palace
figure.means: the ground for Nebuchadnezzar's throne: Babylon's king would conquer Egypt, and his rule would rise on the fall of Pharaoh's

notes.evidence: C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the prophecy rests on a symbolical action: the stones are the base of Nebuchadnezzar's throne, firm against Pharaoh's crumbling clay. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it a visible symbol that his throne would rise on Pharaoh's downfall. Matthew Henry says it is foretold by a sign; Adam Clarke, by a type.
notes.limit: Where the BSB has a brick pavement, most of the writers read a brick kiln, with clay or mortar beside it. Either way, the act means what God says in verse 10.

cites.quote: This prophecy is introduced by a symbolical action, on which it is based. ... The stones must thus form the basis for the throne ... Pharaoh's dominion is like crumbling clay, the material of bricks; the throne which Nebuchadnezzar shall set up opposite the clay-building of the Pharaohs rests on large stones, - his rule will be powerful and permanent.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: stones--to be laid as the foundation beneath Nebuchadnezzar's throne ( Jer 43:10 ). ... Of the same materials as that of which Pharaoh's house was built, the substructure of Nebuchadnezzar's throne should be constructed. By a visible symbol implying that the throne of the latter shall be raised on the downfall of the former.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is foretold by a sign. Jeremiah must take great stones, such as are used for foundations, and lay them in the clay of the furnace, or brick-kiln, which is in the open way, or beside the way that leads to Pharaoh's house ... The foundation of Egypt's desolation was laid in those brick-kilns, in that clay.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Jeremiah, by a type, foretells the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, Jer 43:8-13 . This mode of conveying instruction by actions was very expressive, and frequently practiced by the prophets.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: A scroll tied to a stone and sunk in the Euphrates
notes.about: Jeremiah writes the disaster coming on Babylon in a scroll and sends it with Seraiah. In Babylon he is to read it, tie a stone to it, throw it into the Euphrates and say, “In the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again.” Revelation 18:21 pictures Babylon's fall by a like act.

figure.name: Acted sign
figure.words: tie a stone to it and cast it into the Euphrates
figure.means: Babylon sinking under God's judgment, never to rise again, as verse 64 says

notes.evidence: R. Payne Smith (Barnes' Notes) calls the sinking a symbolic act, the stone signifying the city's sure and swift ruin. C. F. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): a symbolic action showing that Babylon would not rise again. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): a symbol of Babylon's fate. Matthew Henry: a confirming sign. Adam Clarke: the emblem of its ruin.
notes.limit: The scroll was not sunk to be rid of it, two writers stress, but to picture the prophecy coming true.

cites.quote: Jer 51:62-64 The sinking of the scroll was not for the purpose of destroying it, but was a symbolic act (compare the marginal reference); and the binding of a stone to it signified the certainty of the hasty ruin of the city.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This was to be done, not for the purpose of destroying the book (which certainly took place, but was not the object for which it was sunk), but in order to symbolize the fulfilment of the prophecy against Babylon. ... thus indicating by symbol that Babylon would not rise again.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Though he was to throw it into the Euphrates, a symbol of Babylon's fate, no doubt he retained the substance in memory, so as to be able orally to communicate it to his countrymen. ... fourth year--so that Jeremiah's prediction of Babylon's downfall was thus solemnly written and sealed by a symbolical action, six whole years before the capture of Jerusalem by the Babylonians.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He must then tie a stone to the book and throw it into the midst of the river Euphrates, as a confirming sign of the things contained in it ... In the sign it was the stone that sunk the book, which otherwise would have swum. But in the thing signified it was rather the book that sunk the stone; it was the divine sentence passed upon Babylon in this prophecy that sunk that city
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: Thus shall Babylon sink, etc. - This is the emblem of its overthrow and irretrievable ruin. See Rev 18:21 , where we find that this is an emblem of the total ruin of mystical Babylon.
